entries.name: Support vector data description
entries.definition: A one-class support-estimation algorithm that learns a sphere in an input or kernel feature space by minimizing squared radius plus linearly penalized nonnegative distance-constraint violations, then accepts a query when its feature lies within or on the learned sphere.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers the target-only linear-slack method called support vector domain description in 1999 and support vector data description in 2004, with later qualifications to its optimization. L1 refers to the slack loss, not an L1 norm on the sphere center. The negative-example extension and squared-hinge-loss variant change the optimization and are not exact aliases. Sphere support estimation does not include SVC graph-component labeling or the general origin-separating one-class hyperplane formulation. Compared all 442 pinned AIO IDs, labels and scoped synonyms with all 502 preceding native IDs, names and aliases. No normalized candidate identity collision was found. claims.statement: For N target observations and C>0, use squared radius t>=0, center a and slacks xi_i>=0 to minimize t+C*sum_i xi_i subject to ||Phi(x_i)-a||²<=t+xi_i. This is a convex reformulation of the radius-variable problem and satisfies a strict-feasibility condition supporting strong duality. The objective penalizes violation magnitudes, not an exact count of rejected examples. The optimal center is unique, but the radius and slacks can have multiple optima.

evidence.locator: Section 2.1, printed pp.47-49 / PDF pp.3-5, Equations 1-15
Sections 2.2-3.1, PDF pp.4-7, Equation 7, Theorem 2 and Corollary 1; Appendix A, pp.15-16

claims.statement: For C>1/N, the usual dual maximizes sum_i alpha_i*K_ii-alpha^T*K*alpha subject to sum_i alpha_i=1 and 0<=alpha_i<=C, and a=sum_i alpha_i*Phi(x_i). For 0<C<1/N this equality-simplex dual is infeasible even though the primal is feasible: its optimum has t=0 and the feature-space sample mean as center. At C=1/N the same zero-radius solution is optimal, but additional positive-radius optima may exist. Dividing the original radius stationarity equation by R silently omits R=0. For C>1 the method reduces to the minimum sphere enclosing all training features.

evidence.locator: Sections 2.3 and 3.2, PDF pp.5-11, Theorems 4 and 6, Equations 9-26; Appendices B and D, pp.16-17

claims.statement: For C>1/N and an optimal dual solution, squared distances d_i² to the center bound an optimal t by max_{alpha_i<C} d_i² <= t <= min_{alpha_i>0} d_i². A free coefficient 0<alpha_i<C fixes the radius; otherwise choosing the interval midpoint is an implementation convention. Bounded coefficients need not be strictly outside the sphere. Accept a query when K(x,x)-2*sum_i alpha_i*K(x_i,x)+alpha^T*K*alpha<=t. For observations {-2,-1,1,2} with a linear kernel and C=1/2, a=0 and every t in [1,4] achieves objective 4; this illustrates different acceptance regions at the same optimum.

evidence.locator: Section 2.1, printed p.49 / PDF p.5, Equations 14-15
Section 3.2, PDF pp.9-11, Theorem 5 and Equations 20-23; Appendix A, p.16, Equation 41; Appendix C, p.17

claims.statement: A Gaussian kernel exp(-||x-y||²/s²) gives a weighted kernel-score acceptance region without explicitly constructing features. It can produce a non-spherical region in input space. The narrow-width equal-weight limit assumes distinct training inputs; the exact constant-kernel limit is degenerate and does not select a unique coefficient vector. Comparisons with one-class hyperplane support estimation require the stated kernel/normalization conditions rather than general method identity. The boundary estimate is not by itself a normalized density model or a component-labeling rule.

evidence.locator: Sections 2.1 and 2.3, printed pp.50-54 / PDF pp.6-10, Equations 16-21 and 30-35; curator constant-Gram qualification

claims.statement: The papers use support-vector fractions to guide target-error and kernel-width choices. The 2004 account distinguishes essential from nonessential vectors and gives a leave-one-out bound/estimate; the raw support fraction is not universally equal to observed leave-one-out rejection or a calibrated future error rate. With two identical training features and C=2, a valid two-support-vector representation has radius zero, while either leave-one-out fit accepts the omitted duplicate. For the nonnegative equality-simplex coefficients the fraction at the upper bound is at most 1/(N*C); bounded coefficients can be on the boundary, and this count bound cannot be transferred unchanged to signed negative-example coefficients.

evidence.locator: Section 4, printed pp.1194-1195 / PDF pp.4-5, Equation 11
Section 2.4, printed pp.55-56 / PDF pp.11-12, Equation 36; curator duplicate-feature and coefficient-sum calculations

claims.statement: The published tests depend on target/negative sampling, feature dimension, preprocessing, kernel width and target-rejection settings. The 2004 paper reports failures when a pump training set covers too little operating range and cautions that overlapping negative examples can worsen its separate negative-example extension. Its reverse distance constraints are not the convex target-only formulation above. These studies do not establish universal performance superiority or immunity to distribution changes.

definition_evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.11-14, Equations 27-37 and Theorems 7-8; Appendices E-F, pp.17-20

claims.statement: For C>0, minimize t+C*sum_i xi_i² subject to t>=0 and ||Phi(x_i)-a||²<=t+xi_i. Explicit nonnegativity constraints on xi are redundant at an optimum: a negative slack can be replaced by zero to improve the objective. This convex formulation has strong duality and a unique optimal center, squared radius and slack vector. Its squared violation penalty changes the method, even though both SVDD variants use squared Euclidean distances.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF p.12, Equation 27 and Theorem 7; Appendix E, pp.17-18

claims.statement: First consider the zero-radius auxiliary problem minimizing sum_i ||Phi(x_i)-a||^4, with optimal squared distances xi_i*. When their sum is positive, define C*=1/(2*sum_i xi_i*). For 0<C<=C*, the optimal squared radius is zero and the auxiliary center is optimal; for C>C* the radius is positive. This threshold depends on the data and feature map and is not the standard SVDD threshold 1/N. The auxiliary center need not be the sample mean. If all training features coincide, the optimal radius and slacks are zero at their common feature and the denominator formula is inapplicable.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.12-14, Theorem 8 and Equations 28-29, 37; Appendix F, pp.18-20

claims.statement: For C>C*, maximize sum_i alpha_i*K_ii-alpha^T*K*alpha-sum_i alpha_i²/(4*C) subject to alpha_i>=0 and sum_i alpha_i=1. The additional quadratic term makes the maximization objective strictly concave; there is no standard SVDD upper bound alpha_i<=C, though the simplex implies alpha_i<=1. Recover a=sum_i alpha_i*Phi(x_i), xi_i=alpha_i/(2*C), and t=||Phi(x_i)-a||²-alpha_i/(2*C) using any positive coefficient. This equality-simplex recovery is scoped to the positive-radius regime and must not be applied indiscriminately below C*.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.13-14, Equations 30-36 and radius recovery

claims.statement: Prediction compares feature-space squared distance to the learned squared radius, using the kernel expansion when appropriate. A zero-radius fit accepts only queries mapped exactly to the center. The reassessment supplies mathematical derivations rather than a benchmark comparison establishing superiority of squared-hinge SVDD over linear-slack SVDD. Standard SVDD support-count and box-constraint error arguments do not transfer unchanged to this loss. For the symmetric linear-kernel sample {-2,-1,1,2}, C*=1/20; at C=1/10 the solution has center 0, t=3/2 and objective 11/4, as verified by exact KKT and primal-dual calculations.
